start.text: Sister Hild Garrow sits on the kerb of the stage by the skiff with her forearms on her knees, the way somebody sits who has rowed a long way and will row a long way back.
Whoever wants bringing, the Provost said. I'm not to argue and I'm not to hurry them. She's sat on that stage three months. She'll not be hurried by me.

choice.text: Twelve years you rowed out here?
What does the Provost want with them?

twelve.text: Once a month, oil and meal on the stage for the Ridge Light. You'd come back the month after and it'd be gone, every time. Somebody always carried it up. Never saw who; never thought to wait.

Then the Snuffing, and the Provost said nobody goes out in the wet while it's like this. So nobody did. Three months that meal's not come, and three months they've sat here waiting for a boat. We were the boat, near enough. I've been thinking about that the whole way.

want.text: Want? Nothing. To feed them. Kindleby takes in whoever the boats bring; it always has. We took in the Spire's own that came over in the boats, and never asked them a thing.
And the Hushed, in the Quiet House. That's the oldest work there is. But these aren't Hushed. Half isn't Hushed. They'd sleep in the chapter-house by the fire, with us.

kindleby.text: Sister Hild is turning the chapter's skiff over on the shingle to scrape its bottom, her habit tucked up and her arms white to the elbow with salt.

Your colliers keep candles like they were born to it. The big one says forty's nothing and asks for sixty. The thin one stands and looks at the Quiet House. I've told him it's not his business. He says that's what he doesn't like about it.

choice.text: Would you row me out to the Low Water?

home.text: Sister Hild is turning the chapter's skiff over on the shingle to scrape its bottom, her habit tucked up and her arms white to the elbow with salt.
They took the meal and went up the steps, and left me my lantern. Good. I'll row the meal out next month anyway, and leave it on the stage. Somebody always carries it up.

choice.text: Would you row me out to the Low Water?

empty.text: Sister Hild is turning the chapter's skiff over on the shingle to scrape its bottom, her habit tucked up and her arms white to the elbow with salt.
Nobody on the stage. I left the meal anyway, the way I always did. Somebody'll carry it up. Somebody always did.

choice.text: Would you row me out to the Low Water?

never.text: A big sister with her habit tucked up is scraping the bottom of the chapter's skiff where it lies on the shingle, her arms white to the elbow with salt.

Hild Garrow. I rowed this skiff north to the Northing once a month for twelve years: oil and meal on the boat-stage for the Ridge Light. Then the Snuffing, and the Provost said nobody goes out in the wet while it's like this. So she's sat.
I scrape her anyway. A boat you stop looking after starts forgetting she's a boat.

choice.text: Would you row me out to the Low Water?

scraping.text: Weed. The Northing's water grows it on a hull like a beard on a brother who's stopped caring. Twelve years I've had it off her every month, and I'll have it off her now.
Your colliers were good company on the way back, mind. Big one wanted to row. I let him, once.
A clean bottom's a quick boat, and a quick boat comes home. That's all the theology I've got.

choice.text: Would you row me out to the Low Water?

low_water.text: Hild puts the scraper down across the strakes and straightens, a hand in the small of her back.
The Low Water. Who told you of that? ...A Tidewright. They would. They go round it like it's a grave.

I've come by the edge of it. Twice, rowing home from the Northing in a westerly, with the lantern out. You hear them before you lose the light: like the chapter at evening office in the next room, and the door shut. You can't make out the words. You keep thinking you nearly can.

There's a light out there. Lowsong, the old brothers call the rock it's on. A Keeper on it, alone, the way the beacon-keepers are. Nobody's had word since the Snuffing. The Provost wrote them in the Long Book with the rest, and nobody's rowed out to ask.
The Provost said nobody goes out in the wet. Then she sent me north anyway, because you asked her. She'll say yes again. She'll not like it.
The Provost says nobody goes out in the wet. She'll say it again. Then she'll say yes, because it's a Keepers' light, and it's you asking.
But she's to be scraped first, every strake. I'll not take a foul bottom over shallows I can't see. When she's clean, I'll row you. Come and find me.

not_yet.text: Not yet. Another day at her, maybe two. You'll know when: I'll be sat on the kerb with my hands in my lap, looking at nothing, like I've done something.
And you've not been up the steps to the Provost. I'll not row out there without her leave, Wakebearer. Not there.

clean.text: Hild is sitting on the shingle by the skiff with her hands in her lap, looking at nothing. The skiff lies right way up behind her, her bottom black and clean as a boot.
And the Provost's said yes. She sent a novice running down to tell me before you were off the steps. I'm to bring you both back, and I'm not to stop and listen.

row_out.text: Shove her off with me, then. Mind your feet on the weed. What's left of it.

again.text: Hild is at the skiff again, though there's nothing left on her bottom to scrape. She straightens when she sees you.
Back out? She's ready when you are. She's always ready. It's me that has to think about it.

lowsong.text: Hild stands on the landing by the drawn-up skiff, an oar stood beside her, looking out the way the singing is.
I said I'd not stop and listen. I'm not stopping. I'm stood still, which is different.
Is he all there, Iver? ...You needn't say. I saw his hem from here.

row_back.text: Good. In you get. Eyes on the ember, ears to yourself.
